chapter: Newark and first years in Harlem
title: Gershwin's mentor, the old master on St. Nicholas Avenue
summary: Butler tells of an old New Orleans musician on St. Nicholas Avenue (Dave Faulk?) who Gershwin allegedly studied with, his secret polyharmony, and Art Tatum's hidden complexity.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: Was he coming down to the club to see the guys.

He was going -- he was studying with knew up on St. Nicholas Avenue an old man from New Orleans that I / and this old man said that he gave someone his score of 'Afrikana' and I heard that -- I heard what he had in that score of 'Afrikana' and it sounded like a tune that I hear.
Of tunes that I hear around. So that's what the man told me. Now, --
Who was this guy that Gershwin studied with.

This old Dave Faulk, or something like that and he told me, this man -- I would come down by there every night and this master -- see, there's a certain thing musicians about masters that you hear strains coming up you listen.

Yes, and you could hear all these master things and this classic stuff and you -- listen, I knocked on that door. I wanted to know and this big man come in there and the dog wanted to take me out and he told the dog, no, and we became friends, and he told me (unintelligible) but I made a mistake (unintelligible)

And he says, because he was very secretive and he would sit and play that stuff that he---- harmony, big enough harmony, polyharmony but you didn't realize what it is, because he was playing music. You see, when music becomes complete, you don't realize what he's doing in there, because he's doing here, takes all of these surprises out of it. He may playing dissonance up here, but down here, he's got something to take all that surprise out. This is what you hear. You listen to these great pianistsand they be playing all types of things, but it sounds like it's supposed to be there. And there's no name to it. They don't put no tag to it.
For example, Art Tatum was playing all that stuff but it doesn't sound like he's playing, he don't put no tag to what he's doing so this is what I'm saying.
Now, this guy, Gershwin was a student of his.
Yes. I think he went to a German school of Hindemith, because you go to school for certain things and I don't believe that orchestration, for the Rhapsody
in Blue, that Rhapsody in Blue is of an old Hungarian thing.
I don't know too much about schooling up here.
